top_categories.workout_context: Road-specific control matters at L'Étape Mexico City. Practice on mixed terrain: use smooth gear and cadence changes, accelerate deliberately out of corners, and settle quickly back into sustainable power for 68 miles.
Race-pace efforts that mimic L'Étape Mexico City's demands. Pacing, fueling, and tactical decisions under fatigue. Practice the race before November.
When someone attacks on mixed terrain, you have 10 seconds to respond or you're off the back. This builds that response.
72ft/mi signals a climbing-heavy course. Sustained sub-threshold and threshold work builds the steady power needed without turning the opening climb into the day’s hardest effort.
Brief efforts above sustainable power can come from grade changes, positioning, or closing a gap at L'Étape Mexico City. Train them without letting those efforts derail the longer pacing plan.
68 miles on mixed terrain burns energy faster than the distance suggests. Train the fade resistance now.
Steeper ramps, positioning, or pace changes on mixed terrain can demand short hard efforts. Practice them without compromising the sustained work that defines the course.
At L'Étape Mexico City, changes in grade or pace can lift effort above threshold before it settles again. Over-unders train that transition while you keep riding.
88–92% FTP is where you'll spend the hardest sustained miles of L'Étape Mexico City. Train it until it feels boring.
Base fitness for L'Étape Mexico City. Without this, the hard workouts break you down instead of building you up.
Endurance with intensity spikes baked in. Exactly what 4,900ft of climbing on mixed terrain does to your power file on race day.
Varied gradients on mixed terrain demand climbing versatility. Sit the shallow stuff, stand the steep stuff, switch without thinking.
